# The normal distribution {#sec-normal}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Code in this chapter uses **R**.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup-normal
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
bwt <- MASS::birthwt$bwt
bwt_mean <- mean(bwt)
bwt_sd <- sd(bwt)
# share of the birth weights within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean
within_k <- sapply(1:3, function(k) mean(abs(bwt - bwt_mean) < k * bwt_sd))
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
f4 <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)
```

The random variables in @sec-discrete-rv took separate values that could be
listed: 0, 1, 2, and so on. Many quantities are not like that. Heights,
weights, times, and temperatures can take any value in a range. This
chapter shows how probabilities work for such quantities, and introduces the
most important distribution in statistics: the bell-shaped normal
distribution.

## Continuous random variables

### Density curves

A random variable that can take any value in an interval is **continuous**.
You can't list its values in a table the way you did in @tbl-heads, because
there are too many of them. Instead, its distribution is described by a
curve.

@fig-bwt-hist shows the birth weights of `r length(bwt)` babies born at a
hospital in Springfield, Massachusetts.[^birthwt] The histogram is drawn so
that the *area* of each bar is the proportion of babies in that bar's
range, and the areas of all the bars add up to 1. The smooth curve drawn
over the bars follows their shape closely.

[^birthwt]: These data were collected at Baystate Medical Center in 1986 to
study risk factors for low birth weight [@hosmer1989].

```{r}
#| label: fig-bwt-hist
#| fig-cap: "Birth weights of 189 babies, with a smooth density curve drawn over the histogram."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(data.frame(bwt = bwt), aes(x = bwt)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 250, boundary = 0,
                 fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = bwt_mean, sd = bwt_sd),
                linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Birth weight (grams)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```

A curve like this one is a **density curve**. A density curve has two
properties:

1. It is never below the horizontal axis.
2. The total area under it is exactly 1.

For a continuous random variable, **probability is area under the density
curve**. The probability that the variable falls between two numbers $a$
and $b$ is the area under the curve between $a$ and $b$.

This has a surprising consequence. The area above a single point is zero, so
for a continuous random variable the probability of any one exact value is
0. The chance that a baby weighs *exactly* 3,000 grams, to infinitely many
decimal places, is 0. Only intervals have positive probability. It also
means that for continuous random variables
$$
P(X < a) = P(X \le a),
$$
so you don't need to worry about whether an endpoint is included.

### The uniform distribution

The simplest density curve is flat. Suppose a bus comes every 10 minutes,
and you arrive at the stop at a random time. Your wait, $X$, is equally
likely to be anywhere from 0 to 10 minutes. Its distribution is a
**uniform distribution**, and its density curve is a rectangle
(@fig-uniform). The rectangle has width 10, and for its area to be 1 its
height must be $1/10 = 0.1$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-uniform
#| fig-cap: "The uniform distribution of a wait between 0 and 10 minutes. The shaded area is the probability of waiting more than 7 minutes."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 7, xmax = 10, ymin = 0, ymax = 0.1,
           fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  annotate("segment", x = c(0, 0, 10), xend = c(10, 0, 10),
           y = c(0.1, 0, 0), yend = c(0.1, 0.1, 0.1), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10, limits = c(-0.5, 10.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.13), breaks = c(0, 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "Wait (minutes)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Areas of rectangles are easy: width times height. The probability of
waiting more than 7 minutes is
$$
P(X > 7) = (10 - 7)(0.1) = 0.3,
$$
and the probability of waiting between 2 and 5 minutes is
$(5 - 2)(0.1) = 0.3$ as well.

## The normal distribution

### Normal curves

The curve in @fig-bwt-hist is a **normal curve**: symmetric, single-peaked,
and bell-shaped. A random variable whose density curve has this shape has a
**normal distribution**. Normal distributions describe many measurements,
such as heights, birth weights, and errors in repeated measurements, and
they appear throughout the rest of this book.[^normal-history]

[^normal-history]: Abraham de Moivre found the normal curve in 1733 as an
approximation to binomial probabilities, the idea in @sec-normal-approx.
Carl Friedrich Gauss used it around 1809 to describe errors in astronomical
measurements, which is why it is sometimes called the *Gaussian*
distribution. The name "normal" became common in the late 1800s.

A normal distribution is completely determined by two parameters, its mean
$\mu$ and its standard deviation $\sigma$:

- The mean $\mu$ is at the center of the curve, where the peak is. Because
  the curve is symmetric, the mean and the median are equal.
- The standard deviation $\sigma$ controls the spread. A larger $\sigma$
  gives a wider, flatter curve; a smaller $\sigma$ gives a narrower, taller
  one. (The total area is always 1, so a wider curve must be lower.)

@fig-normal-family shows three normal curves.

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-family
#| fig-cap: "Three normal distributions. Changing $\\mu$ slides the curve left or right; changing $\\sigma$ makes it wider or narrower."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
family <- data.frame(mu = c(0, 0, 3), sigma = c(1, 2, 1))
family$label <- sprintf("μ = %g, σ = %g", family$mu, family$sigma)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(family)), function(i) {
  x <- seq(-7, 7, length.out = 400)
  data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x, family$mu[i], family$sigma[i]),
             label = family$label[i])
}))
ggplot(curves, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "darkorange", "grey30")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Density", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

### The 68-95-99.7 rule

Every normal distribution has the same proportions of its area within 1, 2,
and 3 standard deviations of the mean (@fig-empirical):

- about **68%** of the values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean,
  between $\mu - \sigma$ and $\mu + \sigma$;
- about **95%** fall within 2 standard deviations, between $\mu - 2\sigma$
  and $\mu + 2\sigma$;
- about **99.7%** fall within 3 standard deviations, between $\mu - 3\sigma$
  and $\mu + 3\sigma$.

This is called the **68-95-99.7 rule** or the **empirical rule**.

```{r}
#| label: fig-empirical
#| fig-cap: "The 68-95-99.7 rule. The darkest band is within 1 standard deviation of the mean, then 2, then 3."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
bands <- do.call(rbind, lapply(3:1, function(k) {
  x <- seq(-k, k, length.out = 200)
  data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x), k = factor(k, levels = 3:1))
}))
ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = bands, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = k, group = k),
            position = "identity") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, xlim = c(-3.6, 3.6), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#c6dbef", "#6baed6", "#2171b5"),
                    labels = c("99.7%", "95%", "68%"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3,
                     labels = c("μ − 3σ", "μ − 2σ", "μ − σ", "μ",
                                "μ + σ", "μ + 2σ", "μ + 3σ")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

The birth weights in @fig-bwt-hist have mean $\bar{x} =$
`r round(bwt_mean)` grams and standard deviation $s =$ `r round(bwt_sd)`
grams. In the data, `r pct(within_k[1])` of the weights are within 1
standard deviation of the mean, `r pct(within_k[2])` are within 2, and
`r pct(within_k[3])` are within 3: very close to 68%, 95%, and 99.7%.

The rule also explains the guideline for unusual values in
@sec-discrete-rv. Values more than 2 standard deviations from the mean
occur only about 5% of the time when a distribution is normal.

**Example.** Suppose the birth weights of full-term babies in the United
States are approximately normal with mean $\mu = 3{,}400$ grams and standard
deviation $\sigma = 500$ grams. Then about 95% of full-term babies weigh
between $3{,}400 - 2(500) = 2{,}400$ and $3{,}400 + 2(500) = 4{,}400$ grams.
Since the remaining 5% is split evenly between the two tails, about 2.5% weigh
more than 4,400 grams.

## The standard normal distribution {#sec-standard-normal}

### z-scores

The 68-95-99.7 rule answers questions only at whole numbers of standard
deviations. To handle any value, first measure how far it is from the mean
*in standard deviations*. The **z-score** of a value $x$ is
$$
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}.
$$ {#eq-zscore}
A z-score says how many standard deviations $x$ is above the mean (if $z$
is positive) or below it (if $z$ is negative). A baby weighing 4,150 grams
has
$$
z = \frac{4{,}150 - 3{,}400}{500} = 1.5,
$$
so the baby is 1.5 standard deviations heavier than average.

If $X$ has a normal distribution, then its z-scores have a normal
distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. This particular normal
distribution is the **standard normal distribution**, and the letter $Z$
is used for a random variable that has it. Because every normal
distribution can be converted to the standard one with @eq-zscore, a single
table of standard normal areas answers questions about all of them.

### Finding areas

The standard normal table in @sec-appendix-tables gives the area under the
standard normal curve *to the left* of a value $z$, for $z$ written to two
decimal places. To find the area to the left of $z = 1.25$, find the row
for 1.2 and the column for 0.05; the entry is 0.8944. So
$$
P(Z < 1.25) = 0.8944.
$$
You can also find areas with technology: a calculator, statistical
software, or the distribution calculator in @sec-distribution-calculator.

Every question about area under a normal curve is one of three kinds
(@fig-three-areas):

- **Area to the left of $z$.** Read it from the table.
- **Area to the right of $z$.** The total area is 1, so by the complement
  rule, subtract the table value from 1.
- **Area between two values.** Subtract the smaller left area from the
  larger one.

```{r}
#| label: fig-three-areas
#| fig-cap: "The three kinds of standard normal areas: to the left of 1.25, to the right of −0.5, and between −1 and 2."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.4
regions <- data.frame(
  panel = factor(c("P(Z < 1.25)", "P(Z > −0.5)", "P(−1 < Z < 2)"),
                 levels = c("P(Z < 1.25)", "P(Z > −0.5)", "P(−1 < Z < 2)")),
  from = c(-3.5, -0.5, -1), to = c(1.25, 3.5, 2))
shade <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(regions)), function(i) {
  x <- seq(regions$from[i], regions$to[i], length.out = 200)
  data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x), panel = regions$panel[i])
}))
curve_all <- merge(data.frame(x = seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 300)),
                   data.frame(panel = regions$panel))
curve_all$y <- dnorm(curve_all$x)
ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = shade, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = curve_all, aes(x = x, y = y), linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3) +
  labs(x = "z", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

For the three areas in @fig-three-areas:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Z < 1.25) &= 0.8944, \\
P(Z > -0.50) &= 1 - 0.3085 = 0.6915, \\
P(-1.00 < Z < 2.00) &= 0.9772 - 0.1587 = 0.8185.
\end{aligned}
$$
Drawing a quick sketch of the curve and shading the area you want is the
best way to avoid mistakes, such as subtracting from 1 when you shouldn't.

::: {.callout-note}
## Rounding
Table areas have four decimal places, so answers found from the table can
differ in the last digit from answers found with technology. The last
area above is 0.8186 when computed directly, for example. Either answer is
fine.
:::

## Working with any normal distribution

### Finding probabilities

To find a probability for any normal random variable $X$:

1. Sketch the normal curve, mark the mean, and shade the area you want.
2. Convert each value of $x$ to a z-score with @eq-zscore.
3. Find the area under the standard normal curve as in
   @sec-standard-normal.

**Example.** Continue with birth weights, normal with $\mu = 3{,}400$ grams
and $\sigma = 500$ grams. A baby is said to have a *low birth weight* if it
weighs less than 2,500 grams. What proportion of full-term babies have low
birth weight?

The z-score of 2,500 is $z = (2{,}500 - 3{,}400)/500 = -1.80$, so
$$
P(X < 2{,}500) = P(Z < -1.80) = 0.0359.
$$
About 3.6% of full-term babies have low birth weight.

**Example.** What proportion of babies weigh between 3,000 and 4,000 grams?
The z-scores are $(3{,}000 - 3{,}400)/500 = -0.80$ and
$(4{,}000 - 3{,}400)/500 = 1.20$, so
$$
P(3{,}000 < X < 4{,}000) = P(-0.80 < Z < 1.20) = 0.8849 - 0.2119 = 0.6730.
$$

### Finding values from areas

Sometimes the question runs the other way: you know an area and want the
value that cuts it off. Then you work through the steps in reverse:

1. Sketch the curve and shade the given area.
2. Find the z-score with that area *to its left*: look for the area in the
   body of the table, and read off $z$ from the row and column.
3. Convert back from $z$ to $x$ by solving @eq-zscore for $x$:
$$
x = \mu + z\sigma.
$$ {#eq-z-to-x}

**Example.** A hospital gives extra attention to the lightest 5% of
full-term babies. Below what weight does a baby get extra attention?

The area to the left is 0.05. The table has no entry of exactly 0.0500; the
closest entries are 0.0505 at $z = -1.64$ and 0.0495 at $z = -1.65$, which
are equally close, so use the value halfway between, $z = -1.645$. Then
$$
x = 3{,}400 + (-1.645)(500) = 2{,}577.5 \text{ grams}.
$$
Babies weighing less than about 2,578 grams get extra attention.

**Example.** How heavy must a baby be to be in the heaviest 10%? The area to
the *right* of the value is 0.10, so the area to its left is 0.90. The
closest table entry is 0.8997, at $z = 1.28$, and
$$
x = 3{,}400 + 1.28(500) = 4{,}040 \text{ grams}.
$$

Two z-values come up so often in later chapters that they are worth
remembering: $z = 1.645$ has 5% of the area to its right, and $z = 1.96$
has 2.5% of the area to its right, so the middle 95% of a standard normal
distribution lies between $-1.96$ and $1.96$.

## Normal approximation to the binomial {#sec-normal-approx}

### When a binomial distribution looks normal

@fig-binom-shapes showed that binomial distributions become more
bell-shaped as the number of trials $n$ grows. When $n$ is large, you can
approximate binomial probabilities with a normal curve that has the same
mean and standard deviation as the binomial distribution, from
@eq-binomial-mean:
$$
\mu = np, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{np(1 - p)}.
$$
The approximation works well when you expect at least 10 successes and at
least 10 failures:
$$
np \ge 10 \quad \text{and} \quad n(1 - p) \ge 10.
$$

```{r}
#| label: setup-coin
#| echo: false
coin_exact <- sum(dbinom(60:100, 100, 0.5))
coin_cc <- pnorm(1.9, lower.tail = FALSE)
coin_plain <- pnorm(2, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

**Example.** You flip a fair coin 100 times. What is the probability of 60
or more heads? The number of heads $X$ is binomial with $n = 100$ and
$p = 0.5$. Since $np = n(1 - p) = 50$, both at least 10, a normal
approximation is reasonable, with
$$
\mu = 100(0.5) = 50, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{100(0.5)(0.5)} = 5.
$$
@fig-coin-approx shows how closely the normal curve follows the binomial
probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: fig-coin-approx
#| fig-cap: "The binomial distribution of the number of heads in 100 flips of a fair coin, with the normal curve for $\\mu = 50$ and $\\sigma = 5$. The darker bars are 60 or more heads."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
coin <- data.frame(x = 30:70)
coin$p <- dbinom(coin$x, 100, 0.5)
coin$tail <- coin$x >= 60
ggplot(coin, aes(x = x, y = p)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = tail), width = 1, colour = "white", show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 50, sd = 5), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey75", "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Number of heads, x", y = "P(X = x)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### The continuity correction

Look at the bars in @fig-coin-approx. The bar for 60 heads is centered at
60, so it runs from 59.5 to 60.5. To include the whole bar for 60 in the
area under the curve, start the area at 59.5, not at 60. Widening or
narrowing an interval by 0.5 in this way is called the **continuity
correction**.

With the continuity correction, the z-score is $(59.5 - 50)/5 = 1.90$, and
$$
P(X \ge 60) \approx P(Z > 1.90) = 1 - 0.9713 = 0.0287.
$$
The exact binomial probability, from @eq-binomial and a lot of
computation, is `r f4(coin_exact)`, so the approximation is very good.
Without the continuity correction you would use $z = 2.00$ and get
`r f4(coin_plain)`, which is noticeably less accurate.

To decide which way to move, think about which bars you want: "60 or more"
includes the bar for 60, so start at 59.5; "more than 60" does not, so start
at 60.5.

## Assessing normality {#sec-assessing-normality}

Many methods in later chapters assume that data come from a normal
distribution. How can you tell whether they do? No real data set is
exactly normal, so the question is whether the data are *close enough*.

A histogram is the first check: it should be roughly symmetric and
bell-shaped, without strong skewness or outliers. But histograms of small
data sets are hard to judge, and their shape can change with the choice of
bins.

A **normal quantile plot** (also called a **normal probability plot** or
**QQ plot**) is a better tool. It plots each data value against the z-score
you would *expect* it to have if the data came from a normal distribution.
The smallest value is paired with a z-score near the bottom of the
standard normal curve, the median with $z = 0$, the largest with a z-score
near the top, and so on.

If the data are close to normal, the points fall close to a straight line.
Points that bend away from the line show departures from normality: a
curve shows skewness, and isolated points far from the line are outliers.

@fig-qq shows two examples. The birth weights from @fig-bwt-hist follow
their line closely, so a normal model fits them well. The lengths of 141
major North American rivers are strongly skewed to the right: most rivers
are moderately long and a few are very long. The points bend sharply upward,
and a normal model would be a poor choice.

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| fig-cap: "Normal quantile plots of birth weights (left) and river lengths (right). Points close to the line suggest a normal distribution."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
qq <- rbind(data.frame(value = bwt, data = "Birth weights (grams)"),
            data.frame(value = rivers, data = "River lengths (miles)"))
ggplot(qq, aes(sample = value)) +
  stat_qq(colour = "steelblue", size = 1.2) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "grey30") +
  facet_wrap(~data, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Expected z-score", y = "Data value") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Small departures from the line are normal, especially at the ends. Look for
a clear pattern, not perfection.

## Exercises

Use the standard normal table in @sec-appendix-tables or technology, such
as the distribution calculator in @sec-distribution-calculator.

### Continuous random variables

1. A random number generator gives a number $X$ uniformly distributed
   between 0 and 1.
   a. Sketch the density curve and give its height.
   b. Find $P(X < 0.25)$.
   c. Find $P(0.3 < X < 0.9)$.
   d. Find $P(X = 0.5)$.

2. An elevator takes between 0 and 4 minutes to arrive, and its waiting time
   is uniformly distributed.
   a. What is the height of the density curve?
   b. Find the probability that you wait more than 3 minutes.
   c. Find the waiting time that is exceeded only 10% of the time.

### The normal distribution

3. Scores on a standardized test are normal with mean 500 and standard
   deviation 100. Use the 68-95-99.7 rule to answer:
   a. About what percentage of scores are between 400 and 600?
   b. About what percentage are above 700?
   c. Between what two scores do the middle 95% fall?

4. Two normal curves have the same mean. One has standard deviation 5 and
   the other has standard deviation 10. Which curve is taller? Explain why.

5. The lengths of pregnancies are approximately normal with mean 266 days
   and standard deviation 16 days. Use the 68-95-99.7 rule to find the
   approximate percentage of pregnancies that last
   a. less than 250 days;
   b. between 234 and 298 days;
   c. more than 314 days.

### The standard normal distribution

6. Find each area under the standard normal curve, and draw a sketch for
   each.
   a. To the left of $z = 0.87$.
   b. To the right of $z = 1.50$.
   c. To the right of $z = -2.10$.
   d. Between $z = -1.23$ and $z = 0.45$.

7. Find the value of $z$ such that
   a. the area to its left is 0.9505;
   b. the area to its right is 0.0228;
   c. the middle 90% of the area is between $-z$ and $z$.

8. Explain why $P(Z < 0) = 0.5$ without using the table.

### Working with any normal distribution

9. Adult women's heights are approximately normal with mean 64 inches and
   standard deviation 2.8 inches.
   a. Find the z-score of a woman 70 inches tall. Is her height unusual?
   b. What proportion of women are shorter than 60 inches?
   c. What proportion are between 62 and 68 inches tall?
   d. How tall must a woman be to be in the tallest 5%?

10. The time to complete a statistics exam is normal with mean 52 minutes
    and standard deviation 8 minutes. The exam period is 60 minutes.
    a. What proportion of students don't finish in time?
    b. How long should the exam period be so that 99% of students finish?

11. A machine fills bags of chips with a mean of 10.2 ounces and a standard
    deviation of 0.1 ounce, and the weights are normal. The bags are
    labeled 10 ounces.
    a. What proportion of bags weigh less than the label says?
    b. The company wants no more than 1% of bags to be underweight. Keeping
       the standard deviation at 0.1 ounce, what should the mean fill
       weight be?

12. On a quiz, Ana scored 82 in a class with mean 74 and standard deviation
    6. On a second quiz, she scored 88 in a class with mean 80 and standard
    deviation 10. Use z-scores to decide on which quiz she did better
    relative to her classmates.

### Normal approximation to the binomial

13. A fair coin is flipped 400 times.
    a. Check that a normal approximation is reasonable.
    b. Find the mean and standard deviation of the number of heads.
    c. Use the normal approximation, with the continuity correction, to
       estimate the probability of 220 or more heads.

14. About 10% of people are left-handed. In a random sample of 200 people,
    use a normal approximation with the continuity correction to estimate
    the probability that
    a. 15 or fewer are left-handed;
    b. more than 25 are left-handed.

15. For a binomial distribution with $n = 30$ and $p = 0.1$, explain why a
    normal approximation is not appropriate.

### Assessing normality

16. A normal quantile plot of a data set shows points along a curve that
    bends upward at the right end, well above the line. What does this say
    about the shape of the distribution?

17. The incomes of households in a large city are measured. Would you expect
    a normal quantile plot of the incomes to follow a straight line?
    Explain.
